Zero point one looks simple. Inside a computer, it never ends.
In binary, one tenth repeats forever, so the machine chops it off.
In 1991, a Patriot missile battery counted time in tenths of a second.
Every tick, its clock drifted about a ten-millionth of a second.
Tiny. But the Dhahran battery had run for over a hundred hours. Three point six million ticks.
Now the clock was a third of a second off.
A Scud covers over half a kilometre in that time, so the radar looked in the wrong place.
The Scud hit a barracks, and 28 American soldiers were killed. The fix arrived the next day.
A reboot resets that clock. But nobody had said how long was too long.
A tiny error isn't small when it repeats millions of times.
